requirements.statement: On every frontend, a page shows a GOV.UK back link labelled 'Back' ('Yn ôl' in Welsh), above the page content, only when it supplies somewhere for it to go. No page shows breadcrumbs, even when breadcrumbs are passed to the layout. On the animals and plants frontends Back goes to the place the trader actually came from, carried between pages in a 'from' query parameter listing those places newest last and holding at most 40 of them. The places a trail may name are the notification's overview, the set's notification list, the INS type question and any page of the journey by its slug; a trail naming anywhere else, an empty trail or one given twice is ignored in full and Back falls back to the notification's overview, or to the place the page names instead. Saving a page adds it to the trail the next page carries, going Back carries the rest of the trail beneath it, and a link with no trail gets no empty 'from' parameter. A page opened from another page returns to it when the request carries a 'return' marker naming a page allowed to open it, and a marker naming anything else is ignored. The trail and the return marker are percent-encoded into the address and join a query string the address already has.
requirements.why: Each page gets one route back (the back link) and one route up (the service navigation), and the trail is what makes the back link lead where the trader came from rather than to a fixed page. This already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-017, repo-insfrontend-p1-023 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-016 render the back link only when one is set, and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-017 shows breadcrumbs are never rendered. repo-frontend-p2-047-m1 and p2-054 to p2-059 and repo-plantsfrontend-p13-073 to p13-077, p13-111 to p13-113, p13-120 and p13-078-m1 give the trail, its places, its 40-place cap, how it grows and unwinds, and the return marker.

requirements.statement: Sign-in hands off to Defra ID with an OpenID Connect authorisation-code request (scope openid offline_access, query response mode, policy b2c_1a_cui_cpdev_signupsigninsfi), naming each frontend's own serviceId and its own /auth/sign-in-oidc callback. On success the organisation the user signed in for comes back through the callback and the user is held in a server-side session. For a user signed in with Rural Payments credentials, the INS sign-in callback looks up the user's permissions from the Rural Payments and Siti Agri APIs with the Defra ID token, because the token carries the role name rather than its permissions.

It also sends Strict-Transport-Security for a year, X-Frame-Options DENY, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, X-Download-Options noopen, X-XSS-Protection and Cache-Control no-cache.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's accessibility suite holds every scanned page to WCAG 2.2 AA. Every test carries the @a11y tag and is reported under that standard, read from the fixture so the title and the rule set cannot drift apart, and every scan passes the five axe tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa and wcag22aa explicitly, because axe's own default leaves target-size out. A scan waits for the DOM and then allows a bounded settling period, scanning anyway if that wait times out; it is recorded against the page's path; a test runs every one of its scans before failing and reports them together with each violation's severity, rule, description, node count and help link, attaching them to the report as JSON; a failing scan fails its test and a test that takes the scan but never runs one fails too. A test is allowed five minutes. Pages whose layout matters at small sizes are scanned again at 320 by 568 and at 568 by 320, and a narrow scan also proves the page does not scroll sideways once its tables are discounted. A scan may be narrowed per page, and the only exclusions are the two conditional-reveal radio groups whose aria-expanded attribute axe rejects and the sign-in stub's own error list: upstream disagreements in code the service does not own. A clean scan is not full conformance, and a state earns its own scan only where its value outweighs the set-up it needs.
requirements.why: Every page this programme changes must keep passing this suite, and a new scan has to be written to these rules. It already exists.

On the animals side no scan covers the permanent address page, four of the five party pickers and four of the five party edit pages, the contact address edit page, the sign-in page or the organisation picker, the add-address hand-off to the address book, or the germinal-products set, and the narrow-viewport scan of the notification list does not check for sideways scrolling. On the INS side the empty dashboard, the empty address book, the address book's load-failure state, the notification type page and every transporter page go unscanned, and the dashboard's narrow-viewport scans do not check for sideways scrolling. The organisation-scoped API refusals are proven by status code only, the sign-in error is proven only for present-but-invalid values, no test drives the organisation picker as a journey of its own, and nothing proves another organisation's user is refused a notification's view page as well as its overview.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's security suite is a traffic-driven OWASP ZAP scan of six services, each its own named ZAP context with its own address: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book. Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through the proxy rather than letting ZAP crawl, so coverage is traffic-driven and the attacking corpus is curated by hand. There are two profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without attacking, and an attacking one that runs only the @active corpus, is deliberate, runs on the compose stack alone and is refused on the deployed platform because its journeys delete records the scan then re-fires with fuzzed payloads. Anything but the exact attacking profile name is treated as passive. Identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, from a context plan registered before any traffic exists; all three plans must declare the same contexts; diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned; the DOM cross-site-scripting rule is off; the uploader and the queue-consuming INS backend are out of scope with their reasons; and the three APIs are scanned because every API client inherits the run's proxy. The attacking corpus drives sign-in and sign-out, a whole submitted journey, the reason-gated pages and a private transporter, amend, copy, cancel and delete, a document upload with its scan and download, a draft validation error, the notification list's search, paging and sorting, the review page's Change trail, and the INS address book's whole record lifecycle with its role filter, its refused hand-off guard and the INS dashboard. A run fails on a FAIL-rated alert from the rules file (an unlisted alert failing only if it is high risk), on a scan that finished at or within half a minute of its 60-minute cap, or on a declared context that saw no traffic; a per-domain run gates only that domain's contexts and is labelled scoped, and an unknown domain is refused by name. Each run clears its report folder but never removes it, writes a landing page before failing with a row per site, its request count and alert counts, publishes ZAP's log and machine-readable report as HTML, and the pass-or-fail decision is made by the suite's own gate rather than by the plans.
requirements.why: Every route this programme adds or changes must be driven through this scan to be attacked, and a new spec has to be written to these rules. The suite already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: The tests repo's security suite meets it today (repo-tests-p11-037 to p11-102, p15-094 to p15-116 and p16-106 to p16-148). No attacking spec drives the high-risk plants journey, so the plants backend is a declared context that nothing reaches and a full attacking run cannot pass the no-traffic gate as things stand; only a per-domain run avoids it. No transporter route is driven through the proxy. Only the refused side of the address book's cross-service hand-off is in scope, because no accepted token can be seeded. requirements.statement: The INS frontend serves a fixed list of routes, all behind sign-in: the dashboard at /, the notification type question at /notification-type, and the address book's list at /address-book, its add, address type, address view, edit and delete pages and its transporter type, private and commercial add and transporter view, edit and delete pages, each id in a path URL-encoded. It also serves /health, its sign-in routes under /auth/ and static files under /public/. Each page answers a GET at its path, and a POST at the same path when it has a form. It owns no notification set, journey, page engine, document upload or event publishing: choosing a type on the notification type question sends the user to the start of the animals or plants frontend, which creates the draft, and a live-animals notification's origin page can open the question for its own notification and come back to it.

requirements.statement: The INS address book always sends the signed-in organisation, taken from the session, to the address book API, and its client refuses to call with none. Every id in its routes is a 24-character hexadecimal record id, and a dead link on a view, edit or delete page returns to an honoured return page, or else to the address book. When the address book refuses a save as invalid, the page shows the API's first message for each field against that field, and only the validated values are saved, with the address's roles and no address type. A rule that depends on a list, such as the allowed countries, is built from the options the form offered. The country list comes from reference data's /countries and is kept for the life of the process; a failed load shows the shared error page with status 503 and is tried again on the next read. A saved form sets a success banner and redirects.

requirements.statement: Every change to the INS frontend follows its build rules. Pages stay inside the GOV.UK Frontend toolbox, with the Ministry of Justice frontend loaded for its sub navigation only. Every template extends the shared layout, puts the error summary above the h1 and carries a hidden CSRF input in every form; fields use GOV.UK macros with their own error message beside them, and a field's name, id and error key stay identical. Each feature owns English and Welsh copy with the same keys. Only shared/paths.js writes the service's own page paths, and controllers put every link a template needs into the view model. A form's POST honours Cancel, validates, calls the service, sets a success banner and redirects, and a failed service call is logged once and shows the page again with status 500 and the recoverable error banner. The service's own JavaScript only initialises the GOV.UK components. A feature never imports a sibling feature, shared code imports no feature, circular imports are forbidden, and each upstream service has a barrel, a real client and an in-memory stub. Text put into HTML is escaped, and every feature's browser spec checks accessibility on its first render and its error state.

requirements.statement: The performance suite signs in as a browser does: it follows a frontend's redirect chain through that frontend's /auth/sign-in, the Defra ID stub's sign-in form (posting the stub identity's CRN 2100010101 and a password) and /auth/callback back to the page asked for. It counts any hop through /auth/, an identity-provider path containing /oauth2/ or /idphub/, or /organisations as sign-in, counts a chain that lands with 200 without showing the form as sign-in, and never counts one that ends in a server error. It tags the post 'sign-in' and any later sign-in as re-authentication, checks that the INS sign-in went through Defra ID, and shares one cookie jar between the INS frontend and the journey frontend so the INS sign-in carries over to the live-animals dashboard.

The suite posts forms url-encoded through the last POST form that holds a concurrencyToken (or the first POST form when none does), with its hidden fields. A stale concurrency token answered with a redirect counts as handled, and a request that is still redirecting after 10 hops fails its check.

requirements.statement: The plants set is mounted at /high-risk-plants, every plants link carries that prefix, and every plants page renders in the shared layout, loading one application stylesheet and one application script module. A notification's list sits at the set's base URL, a new notification is created at /notifications under it, a notification's overview at /notifications/<id> and each of its pages at /notifications/<id>/<slug>, and the journey can also be entered at /start. More than one set can run side by side, each under its own prefix; a request is placed in the set whose prefix is the longest match for its path before routing, a path whose first segment only begins with a set's name being under no set, and its routes, guards and chrome resolve inside that set, while a path under no prefix takes the site-wide chrome. A set must mount at a path starting with a slash and must configure everything the platform requires of it, or it is refused at mount with the missing piece and the call that would supply it named, and asking for a piece of configuration or a prefix the active set never registered fails naming it. Where only one set is mounted, pages built outside a request still resolve to it; where several are mounted and none is active, anything that needs the current set fails naming the sets. A page inside a set renders through the layout that set names, so a set can give its own pages different chrome.
requirements.why: This is how the shared chrome finds each set's home link, current item and error chrome, which the germinal-products set relies on when it is mounted beside live-animals. It already exists.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-plantsfrontend-p13-068 and p13-069 give the URLs under the mount, p13-080 to p13-084, p13-083-m1 and p13-114 to p13-116 the set resolution and its refusals, p13-057 and p13-058 the chrome a page takes, and repo-tests-p14-080 that the plants home is /high-risk-plants.

requirements.statement: Every page of the animals, plants and INS frontends carries a page-maturity banner, a GOV.UK phase banner directly under the Alpha one and above the Back link, saying how settled the page's design is. The four states read 'Exploring' ('This page is an early idea. It may change a lot or be removed.'), 'Detailing' ('We're keeping this page. We're still working out the detail.'), 'Agreed' ('Users and the business have agreed this page. Changes need a reason.') and 'Ready for live' ('This page is ready for live.'), with an orange, purple, teal or green tag and the banner row behind it in the same colour at a lighter tint. A page declares its level in its feature's page descriptor, which travels with its route, and a page that declares none shows as Exploring. A screen reader hears 'This page's status:' before the tag and a full stop after it. The banner is left off an error page and off any route that carries no page descriptor, the whole banner can be switched off for an environment and is on by default, and its prefix and all four states have Welsh copy with the same keys as the English ('Statws y dudalen hon:', 'Archwilio', 'Manylu', 'Cytunwyd' and 'Yn barod i fynd yn fyw').
requirements.why: The maturity banner is how a reader of a page can tell whether its design is settled, which the prototype has no way to express and says nothing about. It already exists on both journey frontends and nothing in the target design or the rulings removes it.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-frontend-p2-071-m1, p2-072 to p2-077 and p2-157 give the banner on animals, its states, colours, screen-reader prefix, where it is left off, its switch and its Welsh copy; repo-plantsfrontend-p13-018 and p13-035 put it between the phase banner and the Back link on plants; repo-insfrontend-p1-022, p1-053 and p1-068 to p1-079 give the same banner on the INS frontend, its sign-in pages at Exploring.

requirements.statement: A refusal is recorded once in the service's logs with the notification id, the route and the keys of the fields refused, never the messages the trader was shown; a refusal that is not the trader's own correctable input also records any reason or ids it turned on. A save that fails on a backend error the trader can wait out is recorded once with the notification id and the failure, and the page answers with its own fallback. A save refused because the notification changed is recorded once with the notification id and the concurrency token the page posted. A save that opens the page asking for a missing earlier answer instead of the next page is recorded once with the page saved, the page opened and the missing answers. A trail or return marker naming anywhere the journey does not have is recorded once a request as a warning, cut to at most 200 characters of what was received, and a page's own named fallback for Back records nothing.

Opening a notification's page by its address shows the standard 404 Page not found page, which leaks neither its Overview heading nor its reference number; on the backend API, reading a submitted notification's fulfilments is refused with 403, every change to a notification (amend, save, submit, copy, soft delete and cancel amend) is refused with 404, and listing notifications by a reference the organisation does not own returns no rows rather than a refusal. The organisation a request acts for is carried on the backend API in its own header.

Where JavaScript runs, the pages get the GOV.UK button, tick box, error summary, radio, service navigation and skip-link behaviours, the Ministry of Justice date picker, and the service's own enhancements, and nothing else: a behaviour is built from GOV.UK Frontend first, then another tested government library, and otherwise goes back to design. Anything a page can only offer with JavaScript is hidden when the GOV.UK JavaScript has not run, so a trader without it is never shown a control that would do nothing, and nothing a trader needs is shown only by script.

Both journey frontends already load their assets and hide their script-only controls this way.

On a page that takes a file, every save button posts the form to the upload path as multipart, so a chosen file is sent whichever save the trader presses, and a page can put a hidden implicit-submit control ahead of its other buttons so pressing Enter in a field activates the control the page intends. Pressing 'Save and return to overview' on any journey page goes to that notification's overview; pressing 'Save and continue' goes to the next page of the journey that applies to the notification, to the review page when none is left, and to the page that asks for a required earlier answer the notification does not have when the next page needs one.

A list of one page or fewer shows no pagination; otherwise Previous shows except on the first page and Next except on the last, with the first page, the pages either side of the current one, the current page and the last page numbered, the current page marked and an ellipsis wherever numbers are skipped. requirements.statement: The INS frontend's hidden Defra ID test pages are not changed by this programme: the sign-in page with its 'Sign in with Defra ID' start button, the signed-in page listing the ID token's and access token's claims and the token response, and the signed-out page. They are English-only internal pages linked from nowhere in the service, served only when the Defra ID discovery settings are configured and discovery succeeds, and they never change the service's own signed-in identity.
requirements.why: These are internal diagnostic pages for checking the real Defra ID in CDP dev, not pages a trader sees, so the design has nothing to say about them.

requirements.statement: The INS frontend's temporary address lookup spike, a page served only in the dev and local environments that searches by postcode or free text through the INS backend and saves nothing, is not changed by this programme, and neither are the gaps it shows between the lookup's results and the address form.
requirements.why: Address search waits until the INS address lookup is a real feature, and until then every add-address page offers manual entry only.

conflicts.about: Whether the service navigation keeps a Log out item: the target design drops it, and the deployed services have it.

positions.says: In DR2.1 the service navigation has no Log out item, unlike design release 2.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as authentication, overrides the prototype default.
DR1 judged that sign-out sits in the service navigation as 'Log out', replacing the separate 'Sign out' link.
The Log out navigation link signs the user out at /auth/sign-out.
The INS Log out navigation link goes to /auth/sign-out.

conflicts.outcome: Log out stays as the last navigation item on every frontend: both animals sets, the INS frontend and the plants frontend (req-969, req-1674, req-965). The prototype has no real session to end, so leaving it out does not show a decision about sign-out. In the deployed services, Log out is the only way to end a Defra ID session, and the ruling lets an authentication constraint override the prototype. The rest of the prototype's list (Dashboard, Templates, Address book, Manage account) is adopted, so prototype-dr2-1-source-p1-103 still backs the Templates requirement. Only the claim that drops Log out is set aside.

conflicts.about: Where the Address book navigation item goes: inside the same service, as the single-service design has it, or the INS frontend's address book in the deployed services.

positions.says: The design's service navigation lists Address book among its own items, beside Dashboard and Templates, inside the one prototype service.
Rhys ruled that the dashboard and the address book are temporary in the animals frontend and move to trade-imports-ins-frontend.
Cross-service behaviour the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default.
The prototype never decides architecture: the split into services and URL paths stay the deployed services'.
c-213 is kept for a real constraint or a DR1 judgement.
The Address book navigation link goes to the INS address book.

conflicts.outcome: The Address book item goes to the INS frontend's address book from the animals frontend, in both animals sets, and from the INS frontend (req-1677). The address book is a shared capability in a separate service, which the single-service prototype cannot express, and the owner's later ruling keeps this conflict and says the prototype never decides services or URL paths. The item, its label and its place in the order still stand, so the prototype's navigation claim is not set aside, and the claim that placed the address book under the prototype's own base path is no longer in this area's working set, so nothing is overruled. Plants is not wired to the INS address book, so its item keeps the destination its page context supplies (req-2084). Rhys's DR1 judgement still moves the address book to the INS frontend, though the 9 October afternoon and templates rulings keep the notification lists in their own frontends (c-314).

conflicts.about: Where the GOV.UK header logo links: the target design sends it to its index of design releases, which has no counterpart in a deployed service.

positions.says: The GOV.UK logo links to the service index at /index.
The service name in the service navigation links to the dashboard.
The GOV.UK header's crown links to https://www.gov.uk/.
The service name in the navigation links to the page's home URL, which on a journey page is the set's own notification list.
The GOV.UK header's crown logo links to https://www.gov.uk/.
A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.
c-214 is kept for a real constraint or a DR1 judgement.

conflicts.outcome: Keep the current targets, as the owner's later ruling confirms. The GOV.UK logo links to https://www.gov.uk/ on every frontend, as the GOV.UK header pattern does. The service name links to the dashboard home of the set or frontend the page belongs to: the live-animals set's root on live-animals pages, the germinal set's root on germinal-products pages, the plants set's root on plants pages and / on the INS frontend (req-1680). The design now agrees on the service name, which it links to its own dashboard. Only the logo still differs: the design sends it to its index of design releases, which is prototype tooling that is not built (req-1681), so it names no real destination, and with no DR1 judgement on the header the deployed target stands. The design's logo claim is set aside.

conflicts.about: Where the phase banner's feedback link goes: a placeholder in the design, or the APHA service desk mailbox in the deployed services.

positions.says: Because the design's feedback link is a placeholder, DR1 ruled it to be mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk, and forbade inventing a /feedback route or survey URL.
The phase banner's feedback link opens an email to the APHA service desk.
The INS phase banner's feedback link opens an email to APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk.

conflicts.outcome: The feedback link stays mailto:APHAServiceDesk@apha.gov.uk on every frontend, plants included (req-1684). DR1 already judged this same difference, a placeholder feedback link in the design, and a DR1 judgement on the same difference outranks the prototype. The INS and plants frontends already use the same destination. The trace claim that recorded the design's placeholder is no longer in this area's working set, so nothing is overruled; the Alpha banner itself is shown by today's claims (req-2119).

conflicts.about: Whether service pages show the signed-in user's email and Home and About links, as the tests repo's INS page object describes.

positions.says: The INS service navigation has four links, Dashboard, Address book, Manage account and Log out, and the display name it works out is not shown by the layout.
The signed-in user's display name is worked out from the session but not shown in the layout.
No page shows the signed-in user's name or email address, and there is no user header band.
Every INS page carries Home, About, Address book and Dashboard links, the signed-in user's email and a Log out link.

Open: the end-to-end tests still look for a 'Sign out' link and the signed-in email on the notification dashboard, and the action was to point sign-out at 'Log out' and delete the test that displays the signed-in user.
The signed-in identity strip was removed, so the service no longer shows the signed-in user's email or display name, matching the design, which shows no signed-in identity.

conflicts.outcome: No page shows the signed-in identity, and the INS navigation holds Dashboard, Address book, Manage account and Log out with no Home or About (req-1702, req-2118). The frontends outrank the tests repo: the INS and plants layouts show no name or email, the end-to-end traces show none (trace-e2e-p1-040) and the tests repo's own dashboard spec asserts no email (repo-tests-p6-074). The INS page object's description is stale and no spec in this area asserts it, so it is set aside; its locators can go whenever the tests repo is next touched. The open item that the suite still looked for a 'Sign out' link and the email is answered by the same outcome.

conflicts.about: What the status strip calls an AMEND notification: 'Amending', as both journey frontends showed, or 'Amend'.

positions.says: The shared strip's 'Amending' label changes to 'Amend' in every set at once.
Plants' status strip tag reads Amend in yellow for a notification being amended.
The animals status tag reads Amend in yellow.

conflicts.outcome: The strip reads 'Amend' in every set, plants included, through the one shared strip (req-2061). The owner's ruling outranked both journey frontends' earlier 'Amending' label, and since then both have taken it: the animals and plants strips and the plants Welsh twin now read 'Amend' and 'Diwygio', so nothing is left to build. Nothing is overruled, because the frontend claims now record the ruling's own wording rather than contradicting it. The notification list card's own tag is not named by the ruling and stays as the list area has it.

conflicts.about: Which environments every link, redirect and form hand-over between services has to work in, and how that is proved, beyond the INS-to-journey hand-over the owner has since settled.

positions.says: Links between services must work in CDP, in the local Docker stack and in the CI Docker stack, all three.
The ruling names CDP as a whole and no environment within it, such as dev, test or production.
The ruling does not say how working links in all three environments are to be proved, so no check or evidence is named.

For the INS-to-journey hand-over, each service takes the other's address from its own configuration, the end-to-end suite proves it in the local and CI Docker stacks, and no new check is built for CDP.
The INS frontend takes every upstream and journey frontend address from its environment configuration.

conflicts.outcome: The 27 November ruling settles the INS-to-journey hand-over: configuration per service, proof by the end-to-end suite in the two Docker stacks and no new CDP check. It does not reach the other cross-service links, such as the animals frontend's Address book item and the address book hand-off back to a journey. For those the 4 November ruling still names CDP as a whole, the programme deploys to some CDP environments and not others, and two readings build different things, so the question stays with a default that says what each part gets.
conflicts.question: Beyond the INS-to-journey hand-over, which CDP environments must every other link, redirect and form hand-over between services be proved in, and what counts as proof there?
conflicts.default: Every link, redirect and form hand-over resolves from the calling service's own configuration with no hard-coded host or port. The end-to-end suite proves each one in the local Docker stack and the CI Docker stack. The INS-to-journey hand-over gets no new check in CDP, as ruled; every other hand-over is walked once by hand on the deployed services in CDP dev and test. CDP perf, pre-production and production take the same configuration and get no proof in this programme.

conflicts.about: Whether cancelling an amendment is confirmed in a dialog over the journey page, as the design's journey pages include, or on its own page.

positions.says: Every journey page of a notification being amended includes the cancel amendment confirmation dialog.
Cancel amendment is its own page, not a dialog shown over the page behind it.
The status strip's Cancel amend link goes to the notification's own cancel-amend page.
The shared chrome shows no pop-up or dialog of its own.

conflicts.outcome: Cancelling an amendment is confirmed on its own page, reached from the status strip's Cancel amend link, and no journey page carries a dialog (req-2539, req-1697). The interaction designer's ruling outranks the prototype and answers this same difference, and the goal keeps confirmations as pages. The prototype claim that puts the dialog on every journey page is set aside.

conflicts.about: How the INS frontend's browser titles are joined today: with hyphens, as its code and browser tests show, or with a pipe, as the end-to-end trace recorded.

positions.says: Every page's browser title is the page title, then the service name, then 'GOV.UK', joined by ' - ', and the browser tests prove it page by page.
INS frontend page titles follow the pattern '<page> | Import notification service'.

conflicts.outcome: The INS titles already use the hyphen pattern the other frontends use, so req-1686 is met and nothing is built. The repo outranks the trace, and its browser tests prove the pattern on six pages (repo-insfrontend-p1-123 to p1-131); the trace was recorded before the change. The trace's pipe pattern is set aside.
